    Blood Vessels

    Hypertensive Vascular Disease

    B1

    What is hypertension? Important causes and complications of hypertension.

    Hypertension is a sustained elevation of systemic arterial pressure, defined in Robbins as a diastolic pressure of 90 mm Hg or more or a systolic pressure of 130 mm Hg or more. In about 90–95% of patients the cause is unknown (essential hypertension), and in the remaining 5–10% it is secondary to renal, adrenal or other identifiable disease. Its major complications are ischaemic heart disease and heart failure, stroke, aortic dissection and renal failure.

    • Blood pressure is a continuously distributed variable, and the harmful effects of pressure rise progressively with no sharp threshold.
    • Both systolic and diastolic levels carry risk.
    • Individuals with systolic pressures below 120 mm Hg and diastolic pressures below 80 mm Hg are normotensive, and the range of 120–130 mm Hg systolic is borderline.
    • Lower thresholds apply when other risk factors such as diabetes coexist.

    Between one-third and one-half of adults in the general population are hypertensive by these criteria, and prevalence and vulnerability to complications rise with age. Because blood pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by peripheral vascular resistance, sustained hypertension reflects an increase in blood volume (mostly through renal sodium retention), an increase in arteriolar resistance, or both.

    Causes

    • Essential (primary) hypertension (90–95%). This is a multifactorial disorder arising from the cumulative effects of many genetic polymorphisms interacting with environmental factors. Family history, twin studies and genome-wide studies (more than 500 variants) support a genetic contribution. Heavy salt intake, obesity, smoking, physical inactivity and stress are the main environmental contributors. A common final pathway is inadequate renal sodium excretion, which expands volume, raises cardiac output and causes peripheral vasoconstriction, so that pressure is "reset" at a higher level to restore sodium balance (resetting of pressure natriuresis). Vasoconstrictive stimuli and structural thickening of the arteriolar wall add to the rise in resistance.
    • Secondary hypertension (5–10%).
    • Renal: renal artery stenosis (renovascular hypertension, in which reduced afferent arteriolar pressure activates renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone), glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis, polycystic kidney disease and other parenchymal renal disease.
    • Endocrine: primary aldosteronism (frequently an aldosterone-secreting adenoma), Cushing syndrome, pheochromocytoma, acromegaly, thyroid disorders, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia or licorice ingestion.
    • Cardiovascular: coarctation of the aorta and polyarteritis nodosa.
    • Neurologic: raised intracranial pressure.
    • Pregnancy-induced: preeclampsia.
    • Drugs and hormones: oral contraceptives, glucocorticoids, sympathomimetics, tyramine-containing foods with MAO inhibitors.
    • Monogenic disorders: Liddle syndrome (gain-of-function ENaC mutations) and defects of aldosterone metabolism (e.g., aldosterone synthase, 11β-hydroxylase and 17α-hydroxylase defects).

    Special clinical form

    • In up to 5% of hypertensive patients the pressure rises rapidly (systolic above 180 mm Hg and diastolic above 120 mm Hg), producing malignant hypertension with renal failure, retinal haemorrhages and exudates, with or without papilloedema.
    • Untreated, it is fatal within 1–2 years.
    • It is often superimposed on pre-existing "benign" hypertension.

    Complications

    1. Vascular: Hypertension accelerates atherosclerosis and damages the walls of large and medium arteries. This leads to aortic dissection and to cerebrovascular haemorrhage. In small vessels it produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis (homogeneous pink thickening from plasma protein leakage and increased smooth muscle matrix synthesis, narrowing the lumen) and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ("onion-skin" laminated thickening in severe disease, with fibrinoid deposits and necrosis in malignant hypertension), as well as necrotising arteriolitis, particularly in the kidney.
    2. Heart: Pressure overload causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (hypertensive heart disease), which can lead to diastolic dysfunction, left atrial dilation with atrial fibrillation, demand ischaemia, congestive heart failure and sudden death. Hypertension also increases the risk of ischaemic heart disease by about 60%.
    3. Brain: Cerebral infarcts and intracerebral haemorrhage (stroke), and multi-infarct dementia.
    4. Kidney: Arteriolar nephrosclerosis with glomerular scarring, progressing to renal failure.
    5. Eye: Hypertensive retinopathy.

    Hypertension is usually asymptomatic until late in its course. Left untreated, roughly half of patients die of ischaemic heart disease or heart failure and about one-third of stroke, and effective antihypertensive treatment dramatically lowers these outcomes.

    Arteriosclerosis

    Arteriosclerosis: definition and types

    Define arteriosclerosis.

    DU07Ja

    Arteriosclerosis literally means "hardening of the arteries". It is a generic term for arterial wall thickening and loss of elasticity.

    What are the types of arteriosclerosis?

    DU07Ja

    There are four general patterns, with different clinical and pathologic consequences.

    1. Arteriolosclerosis. Affects small arteries and arterioles and may lead to ischaemic injury. The two anatomic variants associated with hypertension are hyaline and hyperplastic.
    2. Mönckeberg medial sclerosis. Calcification of the medial walls of muscular arteries, typically starting along the internal elastic membrane. It mostly affects adults older than 50 years, particularly those with renal insufficiency and secondary hypercalcaemia. The calcification does not narrow the lumen and is usually not clinically significant.
    3. Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia. Occurs in muscular arteries larger than arterioles. It is driven by inflammation (healed arteritis, transplant arteriopathy) or mechanical injury (stents, balloon angioplasty) and is a healing response. It can cause marked stenosis and underlies in-stent restenosis.
    4. Atherosclerosis. The most frequent and clinically important form.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 11)p. 448

    Define atherosclerosis (short note).

    5DU26MDU25MDU22MDU18MDU06Ja

    Atherosclerosis, from Greek words for "gruel" and "hardening", is an intimal-based lesion composed of a fibrous cap and an atheromatous core. The plaque contains smooth muscle cells, extracellular matrix, inflammatory cells, calcifications, lipids and necrotic debris.

    • It is the most frequent and clinically important vasculopathy and underlies coronary, cerebral and peripheral vascular disease.
    • The lesions are called atheromas (atheromatous or atherosclerotic plaques). A typical plaque is a raised lesion with a soft grumous lipid core, mainly cholesterol and cholesterol esters, covered by a fibrous cap.
    • Plaques develop and grow slowly over decades.
    • Its major consequences are myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction, aortic aneurysms and peripheral vascular disease.
    • It is driven by an interplay of vessel wall injury and inflammation.

    Arteriosclerosis vs atherosclerosis; complications

    B1

    Difference between arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis. Complications of atherosclerosis.

    Arteriosclerosis is the general term for hardening and thickening of arterial walls with loss of elasticity, and it includes arteriolosclerosis, Mönckeberg medial sclerosis, fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is one specific type, an intimal plaque disease of large and medium arteries made of a lipid core and fibrous cap. Its main complications are plaque rupture with thrombosis and infarction, aneurysm formation, atheroembolism, intraplaque haemorrhage and chronic ischaemia from stenosis.

    FeatureArteriosclerosisAtherosclerosis
    ScopeGeneric term for arterial thickening and stiffeningA specific form of arteriosclerosis
    VesselsArterioles, small arteries, muscular and elastic arteriesElastic arteries and large and medium muscular arteries (aorta, coronary, carotid, iliac, popliteal)
    Layer involvedVariable: intima (fibromuscular hyperplasia), media (Mönckeberg), arteriolar wall (hyaline, hyperplastic)Intima, with secondary damage to the media
    LesionHyaline or onion-skin thickening, medial calcification, or neointimal thickeningAtheroma: fibrous cap, lipid-rich necrotic core, foam cells, calcification
    Lipids and inflammationNot centralCentral to pathogenesis
    AssociationsHypertension, diabetes, age, renal failure, vascular injuryHyperlipidaemia, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, family history, age
    Clinical importanceMostly arteriolar ischaemia (especially renal) Mönckeberg is usually silentMyocardial infarction, stroke, aneurysm, peripheral gangrene

    Complications of atherosclerosis

    1. Stenosis with chronic ischaemia. Slow luminal narrowing (critical stenosis at about 70–75% loss of cross-sectional area in the coronaries) causes stable angina, chronic ischaemic heart disease, intermittent claudication, mesenteric ischaemia and ischaemic encephalopathy. Collateral flow can compensate when stenosis develops slowly.
    2. Acute plaque change. Rupture or fissuring, erosion or ulceration, and haemorrhage into the plaque expose thrombogenic material. The resulting thrombosis, often completely occlusive, causes acute myocardial infarction, cerebral infarction or sudden cardiac death. Thin-capped, inflamed, lipid-rich "vulnerable" plaques are most prone to rupture, often when stenosis was previously only mild to moderate.
    3. Intraplaque haemorrhage, which expands the plaque and may precipitate rupture.
    4. Atheroembolism of cholesterol-rich debris, which causes microinfarcts distally (for example in the kidneys and legs).
    5. Aneurysm formation (especially abdominal aortic aneurysm) from pressure and ischaemic atrophy of the media with loss of elastic tissue, with the risk of rupture.

    Atherosclerosis: pathogenesis

    B1

    Define atherosclerosis. Tell me the pathogenesis of the development of an atherosclerotic plaque.

    Atherosclerosis is a chronic intimal disease of large and medium-sized arteries in which atheromatous plaques, each with a lipid core and fibrous cap, narrow the lumen and predispose to thrombosis. According to the response-to-injury hypothesis, it begins with endothelial dysfunction, followed by lipid accumulation and oxidation in the intima, monocyte recruitment and foam cell formation, platelet adhesion, smooth muscle cell migration and proliferation, and matrix synthesis, all driven by chronic inflammation.

    Pathogenesis

    The contemporary view holds that atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury, driven by modified lipoproteins, macrophages and T lymphocytes interacting with endothelial cells and SMCs. The sequence is as follows.

    1. Endothelial injury and dysfunction. Early lesions begin at sites of morphologically intact endothelium that show increased permeability, leucocyte adhesion and altered gene expression. The three most important causes are haemodynamic disturbances, hypercholesterolaemia and inflammation (toxins from cigarette smoke and hypertriglyceridaemia also contribute). Plaques localise at vessel ostia, branch points and the posterior abdominal aorta because nonlaminar flow turns off atheroprotective genes such as KLF2, whereas laminar flow keeps them on.
    2. Lipoprotein accumulation and oxidation. With chronic hyperlipidaemia, LDL accumulates in the intima and is aggregated and oxidised by free radicals from inflammatory cells. Hyperlipidaemia also impairs endothelial function directly by increasing reactive oxygen species and accelerating the decay of nitric oxide.
    3. Monocyte adhesion and foam cell formation. Monocytes adhere to the activated endothelium, migrate into the intima and become macrophages. These engulf modified LDL through scavenger receptors, which cannot be downregulated, and become lipid-laden foam cells (SMCs can become foam cells by a similar route). Uptake of modified lipid releases growth factors, cytokines and chemokines that sustain a vicious cycle of monocyte recruitment. The early lesion is the fatty streak.
    4. Inflammation. Cholesterol crystals and free fatty acids in macrophages activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, producing IL-1, which activates endothelium and recruits more macrophages and T cells. Activated T cells release interferon-γ, which further activates macrophages, endothelium and SMCs.
    5. Platelet adhesion at sites of injury, with release of PDGF and other factors.
    6. Smooth muscle proliferation and matrix synthesis. SMCs migrate from the media (or arise from circulating precursors), proliferate under the influence of PDGF, FGF and TGF, and synthesise collagen, elastin and proteoglycans. This converts the fatty streak into a mature atheroma with a fibrous cap. Lipid accumulates both within cells and extracellularly, and late calcification follows.

    Infection with herpesvirus, cytomegalovirus or Chlamydophila pneumoniae has been linked to atherosclerosis only circumstantially, and a causal role is not established.

    What are the risk factors of atherosclerosis?

    7DU25MDU22MDU18MDU17MDU08JuDU07JuDU05Ja

    Risk factors usually have greater than additive effects.

    Constitutional (less controllable)

    1. Family history and genetics. The most important independent risk factor. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is a Mendelian example but accounts for few cases; most familial predisposition is polygenic.
    2. Age. A dominant influence; between 40 and 60 years the incidence of myocardial infarction rises fivefold.
    3. Sex. Premenopausal females are relatively protected; after menopause the incidence rises and eventually exceeds that in males.

    Modifiable major

    1. Hyperlipidaemia, especially hypercholesterolaemia. Raised LDL cholesterol increases risk and higher HDL reduces it.
    2. Hypertension. Raises the risk of ischaemic heart disease by about 60%.
    3. Cigarette smoking. Prolonged smoking doubles the death rate from ischaemic heart disease.
    4. Diabetes mellitus. Induces hypercholesterolaemia; the incidence of myocardial infarction is twice as high, and there is a 100-fold increased risk of atherosclerotic gangrene of the lower limbs.

    Additional

    1. Inflammation, marked by raised C-reactive protein.
    2. Hyperhomocysteinaemia.
    3. Metabolic syndrome associated with central obesity.
    4. Lipoprotein (a) and factors affecting haemostasis, such as plasminogen activator inhibitor 1.
    5. Lack of exercise, a stressful lifestyle (type A personality) and obesity.

    Write in short the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis.

    DU25MDU22M

    The contemporary response to injury hypothesis views atherosclerosis as a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury. Lesions progress through interaction of modified lipoproteins, macrophages and T lymphocytes with endothelial cells and smooth muscle cells. The sequence is:

    1. Endothelial injury and dysfunction, causing increased vascular permeability, leucocyte adhesion and thrombosis.
    2. Accumulation of lipoproteins (mainly LDL and its oxidised forms) in the vessel wall.
    3. Monocyte adhesion to the endothelium, migration into the intima and transformation into macrophages and foam cells.
    4. Platelet adhesion.
    5. Release of factors from activated platelets, macrophages and vascular wall cells, recruiting smooth muscle cells.
    6. Smooth muscle cell proliferation, extracellular matrix production and recruitment of T cells.
    7. Lipid accumulation inside and outside cells.
    8. Calcification of matrix and necrotic debris late in the process.

    Key mechanisms:

    • Endothelial injury. The three most important causes are haemodynamic disturbances, hypercholesterolaemia and inflammation. Plaques sit at vessel ostia, branch points and the posterior abdominal aorta, where flow is turbulent.
    • Hyperlipidaemia. It impairs endothelial function through reactive oxygen species. LDL accumulates in the intima, is oxidised and is taken up by macrophages through scavenger receptors to form foam cells, which release growth factors, cytokines and chemokines.
    • Inflammation. Cholesterol crystals and free fatty acids activate the inflammasome, producing IL-1, which activates endothelium and recruits macrophages and T cells.
    • Smooth muscle cells. They migrate into the intima, proliferate and synthesise matrix under PDGF, FGF and TGF-α, converting a fatty streak into a mature atheroma.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 11)p. 451p. 452p. 453

    Atheroma: composition and sites

    B1

    Composition of an atheroma. Common sites of atheroma formation.

    An atheroma has four components: cells (smooth muscle cells, macrophages and T lymphocytes), extracellular matrix (collagen, elastic fibres, proteoglycans), intracellular and extracellular lipid, and calcification in late plaques. It typically has a superficial fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core. The commonest sites are the lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteries, then the coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, internal carotid arteries and the circle of Willis.

    Composition

    A typical atheroma consists of:

    • A fibrous cap at the luminal surface, made of SMCs and dense collagen, whose thickness and collagen content determine stability.
    • A cellular shoulder region beneath and lateral to the cap, containing macrophages, T lymphocytes and SMCs.
    • A necrotic core deep to the cap, containing lipid (mainly cholesterol and cholesterol esters, often crystalline and seen as empty clefts after processing), debris of dead cells, foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages and SMCs), fibrin, organised thrombus in varying degrees and plasma proteins.
    • Neovascularisation at the periphery, and calcification in advanced lesions.

    Some plaques ("fibrous plaques") consist almost entirely of SMCs and fibrous tissue and may be heavily calcified.

    Sites

    • In descending order of severity: the lower abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries, the coronary arteries, the popliteal arteries, the internal carotid arteries and the vessels of the circle of Willis.
    • Upper limb vessels are usually spared, as are mesenteric and renal arteries except at their ostia.
    • Plaques favour the ostia of exiting vessels and branch points, where flow is turbulent.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 11)p. 452p. 455

    Draw and label a typical atheroma / give the morphology of an atheromatous plaque.

    DU26MDU23NDU17Nov

    Labelled structure of a plaque, from the lumen outwards

    1. Lumen, narrowed and eccentric, because plaques are patchy and rarely circumferential.
    2. Endothelium, which may be eroded or ulcerated.
    3. Fibrous cap, formed by smooth muscle cells and dense collagen. A thin cap makes the plaque vulnerable.
    4. Shoulder, the cellular area beneath and to the side of the cap, with macrophages, T lymphocytes and smooth muscle cells.
    5. Necrotic (atheromatous) core, with cholesterol and cholesterol esters, dead cell debris, foam cells, fibrin and thrombus in varying degrees of organisation.
    6. Calcification in late plaques.
    7. Media beneath the plaque, which may be thinned and atrophic.

    Morphology

    • Fatty streaks. Small flat yellow macules of lipid-filled foamy macrophages that coalesce into streaks 1 cm or more long. They are slightly raised and do not obstruct flow. They are present in virtually all adolescents and may be precursors of plaques.
    • Atherosclerotic plaque. Yellow-tan, raised above the vessel wall; a superimposed thrombus over an ulcerated plaque is red-brown. Plaques vary in size and can coalesce.
    • Four principal components. Cells (smooth muscle cells, macrophages, T lymphocytes), extracellular matrix (collagen, elastic fibres, proteoglycans), intracellular and extracellular lipid, and calcification.
    • Fibrous plaques. Some plaques consist almost entirely of smooth muscle cells and fibrous tissue, which may be heavily calcified.
    • Progression. Plaques enlarge through cell death, matrix remodelling, organisation of thrombus and secondary calcification.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 11)p. 457p. 449p. 455

    Name the blood vessels most frequently involved by atherosclerosis, with clinical consequences (common sites).

    DU23NDU18M

    Vessels involved, in descending order of frequency

    1. Lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteries.
    2. Coronary arteries.
    3. Popliteal arteries.
    4. Internal carotid arteries.
    5. Vessels of the circle of Willis.

    Vessels of the upper extremities are relatively spared, as are the mesenteric and renal arteries except at their ostia.

    Clinical consequences

    • Coronary arteries: myocardial infarction, angina, chronic ischaemic heart disease and sudden cardiac death.
    • Cerebral and carotid vessels: cerebral infarction (stroke) and ischaemic encephalopathy.
    • Aorta: aneurysm.
    • Lower limbs: intermittent claudication and peripheral vascular disease, with gangrene in diabetics.
    • Mesenteric arteries: bowel ischaemia.

    What are the complications of atherosclerosis / atheromatous plaque?

    5DU23NDU17MDU07JuDU06SDU05Ja
    1. Rupture, fissuring, ulceration or erosion of the plaque surface. This exposes thrombogenic material and leads to thrombosis, which may partly or completely occlude the lumen and cause acute infarction. The thrombus may organise and become part of the plaque.
    2. Haemorrhage into the plaque. Rupture of the cap or of thin-walled new vessels causes intraplaque haemorrhage; the haematoma may expand the plaque or precipitate rupture.
    3. Atheroembolism. Plaque rupture discharges atherosclerotic debris into the bloodstream as microemboli.
    4. Aneurysm formation. Pressure or ischaemic atrophy of the media, with loss of elastic tissue, weakens the wall and leads to dilatation and possible rupture.
    5. Atherosclerotic stenosis. Slow narrowing of the lumen causes chronic ischaemia. Critical stenosis, a 70% to 75% decrease in luminal cross-sectional area, causes exertional symptoms such as stable angina.
    6. Vasoconstriction at the plaque, which narrows the lumen and potentiates plaque disruption.
    7. Resulting disease. Myocardial infarction, sudden cardiac death, chronic ischaemic heart disease, cerebral infarction, mesenteric occlusion with bowel ischaemia, and intermittent claudication.
    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 11)p. 455p. 457p. 458

    Atherosclerosis: diet

    A6

    How does dietary habit influence the development of atherosclerosis?

    A6
    1. Cholesterol and saturated fats. The central question is whether cutting foods high in cholesterol and saturated animal fats (eggs, butter, beef) lowers serum cholesterol and prevents or slows atherosclerosis in people without previous cardiovascular disease (primary prevention). Lowering saturated fatty acids to the level of polyunsaturated fatty acids reduces serum cholesterol by 10% to 15% within a few weeks.
    2. Polyunsaturated fats. Vegetable oils (corn, safflower) and fish oils are good sources of cholesterol-lowering polyunsaturated fatty acids. Omega-3 fatty acids (fish oils) are considered beneficial.
    3. Trans-unsaturated fats, produced by artificial hydrogenation of polyunsaturated oils (baked goods, margarine), can adversely affect the cholesterol profile.
    4. Dietary fats in general. The contribution of most dietary fats to atherosclerosis is now viewed as minimal.
    5. Link through lipids. Hypercholesterolaemia, especially raised LDL, is a major risk factor, and lowering serum cholesterol slows progression, causes regression of some plaques and reduces cardiovascular events.
    6. Link through obesity. Obesity brings hypertriglyceridaemia, low HDL, diabetes and hypertension, which all raise the risk of coronary artery disease.

    Vasculitis

    B1

    Define vasculitis. Types of vasculitis.

    Vasculitis is inflammation of the vessel wall. It may be infectious, from direct microbial invasion, or noninfectious and immune-mediated. Noninfectious forms are classified by the caliber of the vessel mainly involved: large-vessel (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis), medium-vessel (polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease, thromboangiitis obliterans) and small-vessel vasculitis, which is either immune complex–mediated or ANCA-associated.

    • Vasculitis can be systemic or confined to a single organ, and its manifestations include constitutional symptoms (fever, myalgia, arthralgia, malaise) together with organ-specific features that depend on the vessels involved.
    • The two basic mechanisms are direct invasion of vessels by infectious agents (e.g., Pseudomonas, Aspergillus, Mucor), and noninfectious immune-mediated injury through immune complex deposition, ANCA, anti-endothelial cell antibodies, anti-GBM antibodies or autoreactive T cells.
    • Distinguishing the two is essential, since immunosuppression helps immune forms but harms infectious ones.

    Classification (Chapel Hill scheme, as in Robbins Table 11.4)

    CategoryExamplesKey points
    Large-vessel vasculitisGiant cell (temporal) arteritis Takayasu arteritisGranulomatous arteritis of the aorta and its major branches Giant cell arteritis in patients over 50, Takayasu in those under 50 ("pulseless disease")
    Medium-vessel vasculitisPolyarteritis nodosa Kawasaki disease Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)PAN: necrotising arteritis, not ANCA-associated, one-third hepatitis B–related. Kawasaki: mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome with coronary arteritis in children. Buerger: young male smokers with segmental thrombosing inflammation of limb arteries
    Small-vessel vasculitis: ANCA-associated (pauci-immune)Microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA) Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3-ANCA) Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA in many)Necrotising vasculitis with few or no immune deposits

    Tumors of Blood Vessels

    B1

    Classify vascular tumors.

    Vascular tumours are classified as benign tumours and tumour-like conditions (haemangiomas, lymphangiomas, glomus tumour, vascular ectasias and reactive proliferations such as bacillary angiomatosis), intermediate-grade or borderline tumours (Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8-associated vascular tumour), haemangioendothelioma), and malignant tumours, chiefly angiosarcoma.

    CategoryTypes
    Benign tumours and tumour-like conditionsHaemangiomas: capillary (including juvenile or strawberry type), cavernous, pyogenic granuloma. Lymphangiomas: simple (capillary), cavernous (cystic hygroma). Glomus tumour (glomangioma). Vascular ectasias: nevus flammeus (including port-wine stain), spider telangiectasia, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Rendu-Osler-Weber). Reactive vascular proliferation: bacillary angiomatosis
    Intermediate-grade (borderline) tumoursKaposi sarcoma Haemangioendothelioma (e.g., epithelioid haemangioendothelioma)
    Malignant tumoursAngiosarcoma (including lymphangiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphoedema)

    Benign tumours usually form obvious vascular channels lined by a monolayer of normal-looking endothelial cells. Malignant tumours are more solidly cellular with cytologic atypia and poor vessel formation, and their endothelial origin may need immunostaining for CD31 or von Willebrand factor.

    Ischemic Heart Disease

    Write a short note on angina pectoris.

    DU21M

    Angina pectoris is characterised by paroxysmal, recurrent attacks of substernal or precordial chest discomfort caused by transient myocardial ischaemia (15 seconds to 15 minutes) that is insufficient to cause myocyte necrosis. The pain results from ischaemia-induced release of adenosine, bradykinin and other molecules that stimulate sympathetic and vagal afferent nerves.

    Three overlapping patterns are recognised.

    1. Stable (typical) angina. The most common form. It is caused by an imbalance between coronary perfusion, due to chronic stenosing coronary atherosclerosis, and myocardial demand. It does not occur at rest but is reliably induced by physical activity, emotional excitement or psychological stress. The pain is crushing or squeezing, behind the sternum, and can radiate down the left arm or to the left jaw. It is relieved by rest or by vasodilators such as nitroglycerin and calcium channel blockers.
    2. Prinzmetal [angina from coronary vasospasm] variant angina. An uncommon form of episodic ischaemia caused by coronary artery spasm. The attacks are unrelated to physical activity, heart rate or blood pressure and can occur at rest. It responds promptly to vasodilators.
    3. Unstable (crescendo) angina. Increasingly frequent, prolonged (over 20 minutes) or severe attacks, precipitated by progressively lower levels of activity or occurring at rest. It is associated with plaque disruption and superimposed thrombosis, distal embolisation and vasospasm, and it is a harbinger of myocardial infarction.

    Silent ischaemia is common in the elderly and in diabetic neuropathy, and may present as dyspnoea, nausea and vomiting, palpitations, sweating or fatigue, or with no symptoms.

    📖 From the textbook (Robbins Ch 12)p. 494
